about: Help text for every setting. The plugin shows it as tooltips and checks presets against it (EngineTest check compares it with the blocks). 'short' is one line (for a status bar). 'tooltip' is the detailed text shown when the mouse is over a control. 'default' must match the code. 'min'/'max' are the knob range in the plugin.

preset.label: Preset
preset.short: One complete amp: a list of blocks that run from top to bottom.
preset.tooltip: A preset is one whole amp. It is a list of blocks (EQ, gain stage, sag, feedback, cab IR) that the sound goes through from top to bottom. You can put the blocks in any order and use each kind as many times as you like. Every amp ever built can be described this way: some tone shaping, some clipping, a power supply that sags, and a feedback loop.

name.label: Name
name.tooltip: The name shown in the preset list. It does not change the sound.

notes.label: Notes
notes.short: Your own notes about this amp.
notes.tooltip: Free text for yourself: what the amp is meant to sound like, which guitar it suits, what you changed. It does not change the sound.

chain.label: Chain
chain.short: The blocks of the amp, in the order the sound goes through them.
chain.tooltip: The order matters a lot. EQ before a gain stage changes WHAT gets clipped (cut the bass before the clipping for a tight sound; boost the mids before it for a singing lead). EQ after a gain stage only changes the TONE of the clipped sound, like the tone knobs on a real amp. Put the cab IR last.

panel.label: Front panel
panel.short: The knobs on the plugin's front panel: which setting each one turns (at most 8).
panel.tooltip: Each knob turns one number setting of one block, found by the block's id. Example: { "label": "Master", "block": "master", "setting": "level_db", "range": [-40, 0] }. It does not change the sound by itself. Without a panel, the plugin guesses a few knobs (a tone stack's three knobs, the last eq's level). In the plugin, right-click a slider in the chain editor and pick 'Put on the front panel'.

auto_level.label: Auto level
auto_level.short: On: the plugin sets its output so every amp is about equally loud. Off: output = input (for effects).
auto_level.tooltip: An amp-style preset puts out tens of volts, so the plugin plays a short riff through it and sets its output to about -20 dBFS. That is right for an amp, but wrong for an effect that goes in front of another amp (strings, restring, bow without an amp after them): there the next amp expects your guitar's own level. Off: the plugin adds no output gain at all (0 dB), so with nothing in the chain the output is the input. The Output knob still works.

panel_knob.label: Front panel knob
panel_knob.short: One knob on the front panel. It reads 0 to 10, like an amp knob.
panel_knob.tooltip: A knob is only a handle on a setting that is already in the chain: turning it changes that setting, like moving its slider in the chain editor. The knob reads 0 to 10; the real value is shown under it.

label.label: Label
label.short: The name printed under the knob. Without it, the setting's own name is used.
label.tooltip: Use the name the real amp uses: Gain, Bass, Middle, Treble, Presence, Master. Double-click the name on the panel to change it.

block.label: Block
block.short: The id of the block the knob turns.
block.tooltip: The block can be anywhere: in the main chain, inside a feedback loop or inside a split path. It needs an id; the plugin gives it one when you put one of its settings on the panel.

setting.label: Setting
setting.short: The setting the knob turns, like "level_db". A dot path reaches into a list: "path.0.gain_db".
setting.tooltip: It must be a number setting. Dot paths reach filter bands and split paths: "bands.1.gain_db" is the gain of the second band of an eq, "path.0.gain_db" the first band of a feedback loop's path, "paths.0.level_db" the level of a split block's first path. Counting starts at 0.

range.label: Range
range.short: What 0 and 10 on the knob mean, in the setting's own unit, like [-40, 0].
range.tooltip: Without it, the setting's own range is used (the one its slider has). It can run backwards: a Presence knob is [0, -12] because cutting the treble in the feedback path makes the amp brighter. Values in between are spread evenly, so for a dB setting the knob feels like a real volume pot.

type.label: Block type

choices.tonestack: The real bass/mid/treble circuit of a tube amp, worked out from its part values.
choices.gain: One gain stage: filter, clip, filter.
choices.power: A push-pull power amp: two power tubes (EL34, 6L6GC, EL84, 6V6GT, KT88, 6550) into an output transformer.
choices.sag: Power supply sag: lowers the clipping ceiling of later gain stages when you play hard.
choices.feedback: A loop around a few blocks, like the feedback loop of a power amp.
choices.split: Parallel paths: the same sound goes through several chains side by side, then they are mixed.
choices.gate: Noise gate: turns the sound down when you stop playing, to remove hiss and hum.
choices.ir: Speaker cabinet sound from an impulse response file.
choices.room: Acoustic feedback: the amp's sound goes back into the guitar, as when you stand in front of a loud amp.
choices.strings: Sympathetic strings: extra strings tuned to fixed notes ring along with your playing, like a sitar's.
choices.restring: Your playing plucks a virtual string with physics you choose: lower, stiffer, longer.
choices.bow: Your playing bows a virtual string: long notes that swell and sing, like a cello.
choices.mouth: A vocal tract: the sound goes through a mouth shaping vowels, like a talk box.

type.short: What kind of block this is.
type.tooltip: Each block does one job. Combine them in any order to build any amp.

id.label: Name (id)
id.short: A short name for this block, so other blocks can point to it.
id.tooltip: Optional. Give a block an id (for example "power") when a sag block must control it. Each id must be used only once in a preset. It does not change the sound.

band.label: Filter band
band.short: One filter: boosts or cuts a range of tones.
band.tooltip: A filter band is the basic tool for shaping tone. It is used inside EQ blocks, before and after the clipping in gain stages, and in the path of a feedback loop. Several bands in a row add up.

kind.label: Type

choices.highpass: Removes everything BELOW the frequency. Use it to remove mud and boom. 'freq' is where the cut starts; 'q' sets how sharp the corner is.
choices.lowpass: Removes everything ABOVE the frequency. Use it to remove fizz and harshness. 'freq' is where the cut starts; 'q' sets how sharp the corner is.
choices.lowshelf: Raises or lowers everything below the frequency by the same amount, like a bass knob. 'gain_db' sets how much.
choices.highshelf: Raises or lowers everything above the frequency by the same amount, like a treble knob. 'gain_db' sets how much.
choices.peak: Raises or lowers a range of tones around the frequency, like one band of a parametric EQ. 'q' sets how wide the range is.
choices.highpass1: A gentle 1st-order high-pass (6 dB per octave), like one coupling capacitor into a resistor, or a transformer's low end: 1 / (2 pi R C) gives the freq (22 nF into 1 Mohm = 7.2 Hz). No q or gain_db. Real amps are full of these.
choices.lowpass1: A gentle 1st-order low-pass (6 dB per octave), like one resistor into a capacitor (a treble bleed, a Miller capacitance). No q or gain_db.

kind.tooltip: High-pass and low-pass remove tones. Shelves work like the bass and treble knobs on a hi-fi. Peak changes one area in the middle, like a parametric EQ.

freq.label: Frequency
freq.short: Which tones this band works on.
freq.tooltip: The pitch where the filter acts. Rough guide for guitar: 80-150 Hz = boom and body, 200-400 Hz = warmth or mud, 500-1000 Hz = the 'honk' and the voice of the amp, 1-3 kHz = bite and cutting through a band, 3-6 kHz = presence and pick attack, above 6 kHz = fizz and air. A guitar speaker plays almost nothing above about 5-6 kHz.

q.label: Width (Q)
q.short: How narrow the band is. Higher = narrower.
q.tooltip: For 'peak': a low Q (0.5-1) changes a wide area and sounds natural; a high Q (4-10) hits a small area, good for removing one ugly ring. For high-pass, low-pass and shelves: 0.707 gives a smooth corner with no bump; higher values add a bump right at the corner frequency (the old amp circuits often have such a bump).

gain_db.label: Boost / cut
gain_db.short: How much to raise (+) or lower (-) the tones. Used by shelves and peaks.
gain_db.tooltip: +6 dB is about twice as loud in that area; -6 dB is about half. Small changes (2-4 dB) are often enough. Big boosts before a gain stage make that area clip much more, which changes the character of the distortion, not only the tone. High-pass and low-pass ignore this setting.

split_path.label: Split path
split_path.short: One of the parallel chains inside a split block.
split_path.tooltip: Each path gets the same input. Its own chain of blocks runs on it, then it is mixed with the other paths at its own level.

chain.label: Chain
chain.short: The blocks in this path. Empty = the untouched input.
chain.tooltip: Any blocks can go here, even another split or a feedback loop. A cab IR can not go here: the plugin runs the cab after the amp, at the normal sample rate, so it must be at the end of the main chain. Leave it empty to pass the input through untouched: useful for a clean blend under a distorted path.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.short: How loud this path is in the mix.
level_db.tooltip: Works like the volume knob of one channel in a 'jumpered' amp: turn one path down to hear more of the other. -60 dB is about off. Since paths are simply added, the total gets louder when several paths are up; use the split block's Level to bring it back.

invert.label: Invert
invert.short: Flips this path upside down before mixing (polarity).
invert.tooltip: When two paths are mixed and one is flipped, the tones they share cancel out and only the differences stay. Real circuits do this: some tube stages flip the signal and some do not, so two paths through a different number of stages can partly cancel. Try it when a blend sounds thin or hollow: flipping one path often fixes it (or makes it the special sound you want). Two identical paths with one flipped = silence.

power.label: Power amp
power.short: A push-pull power amp: two power tubes into an output transformer.
power.tooltip: The last tube stage of a tube amp. The phase inverter sends opposite signals to two power tubes; the output transformer passes on only the DIFFERENCE of their currents. Because of that, the even harmonics of the two tubes cancel (measured: 0.00% 2nd harmonic with matched tubes), so a power amp clips with a different, more 'open' sound than a preamp stage. The power tube type is one of the biggest differences between famous amps: EL34 (British amps), 6L6GC (big American amps and many high-gain amps), EL84 (small British 'chime' amps), 6V6GT (small American amps), KT88 and 6550 (big 100 W and bass amps: huge clean headroom). The tube curves are fitted to each tube's datasheet. The plugin shows the idle current and the rough output power of your settings. Put a sag block before it, and usually a feedback block around it.

linear.label: Linear (no clipping)
linear.short: The same stage without its non-linear parts, for comparing (X-ray listening uses it).
linear.tooltip: On: the pair becomes a perfect linear amplifier with the same gain for quiet playing: no clipping, no crossover, no bias shift, no transformer saturation, and its supply never sags. Comparing a stage with its linear twin shows exactly what the clipping does; X-ray listening subtracts one from the other so you hear only that.

tube.label: Power tubes

choices.EL34: British sound: strong upper mids, an aggressive 'crunch' when pushed, breaks up earlier. About 50 W from a pair at 450 V into 3.4k.
choices.6L6GC: American sound: big clean headroom, deep bass, smooth highs, scooped feel. About 45 W from a pair at 460 V into 4.2k.
choices.EL84: Small British 'chime': bright, breaks up early and sweetly, compressed. About 17 W from a pair at 320 V into 8k.
choices.6V6GT: Small American amps: warm, breaks up early and smoothly. About 22 W from a pair at 420 V into 8k.
choices.KT88: Big British and hi-fi 100 W amps: very tight bass, huge clean headroom, hard to push into breakup. About 100 W from a pair at 560 V into 4.5k (datasheet).
choices.6550: Big American amps and bass amps (the 6550 is the American cousin of the KT88): deep, punchy, lots of clean headroom. About 100 W from a pair at 600 V into 5k (datasheet).

tube.tooltip: Each tube's curve is fitted to its datasheet (current and gain at 250 V, matched exactly). Typical safe bias voltages (about 70% of the tube's maximum heat): EL34 at 450 V: -46 V; 6L6GC at 460 V: -47 V; EL84 at 320 V: -13 V; 6V6GT at 420 V: -40 V; KT88 at 560 V: -66 V; 6550 at 600 V: -76 V (with the screen at the plate voltage; real KT88/6550 amps often run the screen lower, then less bias is needed). When you change the tube, change the bias too.

plate_v.label: Supply voltage (B+)
plate_v.short: The power supply voltage on the power tubes.
plate_v.tooltip: More voltage = more clean headroom, more power, tighter bass. Less = earlier, softer breakup. Typical: 420-480 V for EL34 and 6L6GC amps, 300-350 V for EL84 amps, 400-430 V for 6V6GT amps. If you change it, check the bias: at a higher voltage the same bias gives much more idle current.

screen_v.label: Screen voltage
screen_v.short: The voltage on the tubes' screen grids. Empty = the same as the supply voltage.
screen_v.tooltip: In most amps the screens sit a little below the supply. A lower screen voltage gives less current and gain: softer, earlier breakup with less power. Leave empty to use the supply voltage.

bias_v.label: Bias voltage
bias_v.short: The grid voltage at rest. Sets the idle current: 'hot' (closer to 0) or 'cold' (more negative).
bias_v.tooltip: Hot (closer to 0 V): more idle current, a smooth, warm, 'class A'-like sound, but the tubes get hot. Cold (more negative): less heat, but crossover distortion at low and medium volume: a grainy, 'fizzy' edge on quiet notes. Measured with EL34 at 450 V and 10 V drive: -38 V gives 0.24% distortion, -45 V gives 1.6% (crossover). Typical safe values: EL34 at 450 V: -46 V; 6L6GC at 460 V: -47 V; EL84 at 320 V: -13 V; 6V6GT at 420 V: -40 V; KT88 at 560 V: -66 V; 6550 at 600 V: -76 V. The default (-45 V) suits the default EL34 at 450 V (about 39 mA per tube).

raa_ohms.label: Load (plate to plate)
raa_ohms.short: The output transformer's load, seen from plate to plate.
raa_ohms.tooltip: From the output transformer data or the schematic. Typical: 3.4k for a pair of EL34, 4.2k for a pair of 6L6GC, 8k for a pair of EL84 or 6V6GT, 4.5k for KT88, 5k for 6550 (four tubes = half the value). A lower load gives more current and a 'fatter', more compressed sound; a higher load gives more voltage swing and an earlier, brighter breakup. In a real amp, using a speaker with the wrong impedance changes this value.

mismatch.label: Tube mismatch
mismatch.short: How much weaker tube B is than tube A. 0 = a perfect pair.
mismatch.tooltip: Real tube pairs are never perfect. A mismatch lets some even harmonics through (measured: 10% mismatch gives about 1% 2nd harmonic when driven hard), which sounds thicker and a bit rougher, and it adds a small hum in a real amp. 0.05-0.1 is a normal 'real-world' pair.

pairs.label: Tube pairs
pairs.short: How many pairs of power tubes work side by side. 2 = the four tubes of a 100 W amp.
pairs.tooltip: Big amps put two (or three) pairs in parallel: each side's current adds up, and they drive a transformer with half the load (raa_ohms) to get twice the power. Into half the load each tube works just as in a single pair, so the clipping sounds the same; what changes is the power (50 W -> 100 W) and that the power supply has to feed twice the current, so it sags more with the same rectifier. Halve raa_ohms when you go from 1 to 2 pairs (3.4k -> 1.7k for EL34s), as the real amps do.

coupling_nf.label: Coupling capacitors
coupling_nf.short: The capacitors from the phase inverter to the power tubes' grids. 0 = DC-coupled.
coupling_nf.tooltip: With the grid (bias feed) resistors they make a gentle bass cut, 1 / (2 pi R C): 22 nF into 220k = 33 Hz. They also cause the power tubes' bias shift: when a grid is driven past 0 V it charges its capacitor, which drains through the grid resistor in C x R (22 nF x 220k = 4.8 ms). Bigger capacitors: deeper bass and longer 'farting' recovery when driven hard.

grid_ohms.label: Grid resistors
grid_ohms.short: The power tubes' grid (bias feed) resistors.
grid_ohms.tooltip: Usually 220k (sometimes 100k or 470k). With the coupling capacitors they set the bass cut and how fast bias shift recovers.

drive_db.label: Drive
drive_db.short: How many volts reach the power tube grids.
drive_db.tooltip: The input is in volts at each grid. Full output needs about as many volts as the bias (for example 45 V for a -45 V bias); the phase inverter of a real amp gives up to about 50-80 V. So if the signal coming in is around 1, a drive of about +30 to +36 dB reaches full power. In a real amp this is the master volume.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: The output is scaled so that full power equals the bias voltage (for example about 45 at -45 V). Use this to bring it down, for example to about -33 dB to get back near 1.

pre.label: Pre filters
pre.short: Filters before the tubes (the phase inverter's coupling).
pre.tooltip: In a real amp, the coupling capacitors before the power tubes cut some low bass (a high-pass around 10-30 Hz) and that matters a lot for blocking. A high-pass here keeps the power amp tight when driven hard.

post.label: Post filters
post.short: Filters after the tubes (the output transformer).
post.tooltip: The output transformer limits the bandwidth: a high-pass around 40-80 Hz and a low-pass around 6-10 kHz copy it. A 10 Hz high-pass is always added at the end.

oversample.label: Oversampling
oversample.short: How many times faster the tubes run, to avoid harsh noise.
oversample.tooltip: Does nothing: the whole amp is oversampled once (the Quality menu). Kept so older presets still load.

bias_shift.label: Bias shift
bias_shift.short: How much hard playing pushes both tubes colder for a moment. 0 = off.
bias_shift.tooltip: When a grid is driven above 0 V, it charges its coupling capacitor and the tube goes colder; each tube's grid does this on its own half of the wave. Both tubes end up colder, so crossover distortion grows right after hard playing and then fades: the famous 'farty' or 'gated' sound of an overdriven power amp, and part of its 'bloom'. Measured with 0.5: a soft note right after a loud part had 5.4% distortion instead of 3.1%, back to normal after about 250 ms.

shift_attack_ms.label: Shift attack
shift_attack_ms.short: How fast the grids charge when driven above 0 V.
shift_attack_ms.tooltip: Fast in a real amp (about 1 ms). Only matters when Bias shift is above 0.

shift_release_ms.label: Shift release
shift_release_ms.short: How fast the grids recover. Empty = C x R of the coupling capacitors.
shift_release_ms.tooltip: In a real amp: the coupling capacitor times the bias resistor (for example 22 nF x 220k = 5 ms, 100 nF x 220k = 22 ms). Bigger coupling capacitors = longer recovery and more 'farting' when driven hard; that is why some amps use small ones. Only matters when Bias shift is above 0.

supply_ohms.label: Supply resistance
supply_ohms.short: Rectifier sag: the resistance between the power transformer and the filter capacitor. 0 = a perfectly stiff supply.
supply_ohms.tooltip: The power tubes draw more current when you play hard (most of all in class AB), and that current drops the supply voltage across this resistance: the amp 'sags' and compresses, then recovers when you play softly. This is the real cause of tube-rectifier feel. It is the rectifier's own drop plus the transformer winding. Rough guesses (from typical datasheet voltage drops as remembered, not checked against real amps): silicon diodes (the drop is only the winding) about 50-100 ohm; GZ34/5AR4 about 120-170; 5U4GB about 250-300; 5Y3 (small amps) about 400-500. A tube rectifier's drop is not exactly proportional to the current (it grows a bit slower), so this is an approximation. Plate V stays the voltage at idle. The signal view shows the supply as its own strip under the power block.

supply_uf.label: Filter capacitor
supply_uf.short: The first filter capacitor of the power supply: how fast the sag comes and goes.
supply_uf.tooltip: The supply voltage falls and recovers with the time constant Supply resistance x Filter capacitor (for example 250 ohm x 47 uF = 12 ms). A small capacitor makes the sag fast and 'spongy'; a big one makes the supply steadier. Typical first capacitors: 32-100 uF. Only matters when Supply resistance is above 0. (A real supply is also recharged only at the peaks of the mains, 100 or 120 times a second; that ripple is left out.)

preamp_targets.label: Preamp on this supply
preamp_targets.short: The ids of the gain stages fed from this power supply: they sag with it, a little later.
preamp_targets.tooltip: In a real amp one rectifier and filter capacitor feed everything: the power tubes, then (through more resistors and capacitors, the 'decoupling' filters) the phase inverter and every preamp stage. So when the power tubes pull the supply down, the preamp's voltage follows slowly, and the preamp stages clip a little lower too: more compression and 'bloom' when you dig in. The stages can be anywhere in the chain, also before this power block. Needs Supply resistance above 0 (a stiff supply never sags). The signal view's supply strip shows the voltage they follow.

preamp_filter_ms.label: Preamp supply filter
preamp_filter_ms.short: How slowly the preamp's voltage follows the supply (the decoupling filters).
preamp_filter_ms.tooltip: The time constant of the decoupling filters between the main supply and the preamp: resistor x capacitor, for example 10k x 10 uF = 100 ms. Real amps have several in a row (one per stage or pair of stages), so the preamp follows the supply smoothly over 50-500 ms: it does not ripple with each note, it swells and recovers with your playing.

transformer_low_hz.label: Transformer low end
transformer_low_hz.short: Where the output transformer starts to lose the bass (a gentle 1st-order roll-off).
transformer_low_hz.tooltip: The output transformer's winding is an inductor across the speaker load, so the lowest notes leak away through it: a gentle (6 dB per octave) bass cut that starts here. A big transformer: 5-20 Hz. A small one: 30-80 Hz. It also means no DC reaches the speaker.

transformer_sat_hz.label: Transformer saturation
transformer_sat_hz.short: How small the transformer core is: the lowest note it passes at full power before the core saturates. 0 = never.
transformer_sat_hz.tooltip: A transformer core holds only so much magnetism, and the magnetism grows with the voltage AND the time it lasts: so a loud LOW note fills the core much more than a loud high one. When the core is full (saturated), the winding stops working as an inductor: the bass of loud low notes collapses and distorts (odd harmonics), while high notes and quiet playing are unchanged. This is the number: at this frequency a full-power note just reaches saturation; lower or louder notes go into it. A big, generous transformer: 20-30 Hz. A small or cheap one: 60-120 Hz. 0 = the core never saturates.

tonestack.label: Tone stack
tonestack.short: The real passive tone circuit of a tube amp (bass/mid/treble, or bass/treble), worked out from its part values.
tonestack.tooltip: Almost every famous tube amp uses the same passive tone circuit (3 capacitors, 1 resistor, 3 pots), only with different part values. This block works out that exact circuit, so the knobs behave like the real amp: they affect each other (for example, Mid also changes the treble level), there is a built-in mid scoop, and the whole circuit loses volume, as in the real amp. Checked against the published formula for this circuit (Yeh and Smith, 2006): same answer within 0.001 dB. Two other circuits are there too: the 60s British 'top boost' (bass and treble only) and the 'James' bass/treble circuit (a passive Baxandall, flat with both knobs at 5). Where to put it: after the first one or two gain stages in most British and American amps; BEFORE the gain stages in some amps (for example the Mesa Mark series), which makes the knobs change the distortion itself.

style.label: Part values

choices.british: Values like the classic British 100 W amps: C1 470 pF, C2 22 nF, C3 22 nF, treble 220k, bass 1M, mid 25k, slope 33k. Less mid scoop (about -5 dB at 700 Hz with all knobs at 5), punchy mids.
choices.american: Values like the 1959 American tweed bass amp (the circuit the British amps copied): C1 250 pF, C2 20 nF, C3 20 nF, treble 250k, bass 1M, mid 25k, slope 56k. Deeper mid scoop (about -7 dB at 760 Hz with all knobs at 5).
choices.top_boost: The 60s British 'top boost' circuit (chime amps with EL84s): the same circuit without a mid knob. C1 50 pF, C2 22 nF, C3 22 nF, treble 1M log, bass 1M log, slope 100k, and a fixed 10k where the mid pot would be (that value is a guess: check the schematic). Bright and jangly, strong treble range.
choices.james: The 'James' bass/treble circuit (a passive Baxandall, as in many hi-fi and some guitar amps): bass and treble only, both 1M log pots. FLAT with both knobs at 5 (it then loses about 21 dB); bass +-15 dB at 40 Hz, treble +18/-15 dB at 8 kHz, and 1 kHz hardly moves. The part values are a design for this plugin, not copied from one amp.

style.short: Which circuit and set of part values to start from.
style.tooltip: The starting circuit and part values. Any single part can then be changed with 'Parts'. The top_boost and james styles have no mid knob: setting 'mid' with them is an error. The values are from common published schematics; check them against the schematic of the exact amp you want to copy.

parts.label: Parts

fmv.C1: Treble capacitor (farads, e.g. 470e-12 = 470 pF). Bigger = the treble knob reaches lower and the sound gets brighter.
fmv.C2: Bass capacitor (farads, e.g. 22e-9 = 22 nF). Bigger = more low bass.
fmv.C3: Mid capacitor (farads). Bigger = the mid knob works lower.
fmv.R2: Bass pot total resistance (ohms). Bigger = more bass range.
fmv.R3: Mid pot total resistance (ohms). Bigger = more mids overall. In top_boost: the fixed resistor where the mid pot would be.
fmv.R4: Slope resistor (ohms). The most important value for the character: smaller = more mids and more output (British), bigger = deeper scoop (American, and amps with a 100k slope resistor sound very scooped).

james.C1: Treble capacitor from the input to the top of the treble pot (farads). Bigger = the treble knob reaches lower.
james.C2: Treble capacitor from the bottom of the treble pot to ground (farads). Keep it about 10 times C1.
james.C3: Bass capacitor across the top half of the bass pot (farads). Bigger = the bass knob works higher up.
james.C4: Bass capacitor across the bottom half of the bass pot (farads). Keep it about 10 times C3.
james.R3: Input resistor before the bass pot (ohms). With R4 it sets the loss in the middle: about R4 / (R3 + R4).
james.R4: Resistor from the bottom of the bass pot to ground (ohms). Keep R3 about 10 times R4.
james.R5: Resistor from the bass pot's wiper to the output (ohms): keeps the bass and treble parts apart.

parts.short: Change any single part value of the circuit.
parts.tooltip: Only list the parts you want to change; the others come from the style. Units are farads and ohms: 470 pF = 470e-12, 22 nF = 22e-9, 220k = 220e3, 1M = 1e6. This is how you copy one exact amp from its schematic.

treble.label: Treble
treble.tooltip: Moves the output pick-off point along the treble pot. Up = more highs, AND less mids and bass (the knobs share one circuit). Measured with British values and the other knobs at 5: 3 kHz goes from -10.5 dB (treble 0) to -1.7 dB (treble 10).

mid.label: Middle
mid.tooltip: Sets how much the mid pot holds the mids up. Up = more mids AND a louder sound overall, because more of the signal gets through. At 0 you get the deepest scoop and the lowest volume. Measured with British values: 500 Hz goes from -11.8 dB (mid 0) to -6.6 dB (mid 10), and 3 kHz moves too (-8.5 to -4.1 dB).

bass.label: Bass
bass.tooltip: Sets how much low end gets through. Most of the change happens in the top half of the knob when the taper is 'log' (like the real audio-taper pot). Measured with British values: 100 Hz goes from -10.7 dB (bass 0) to -2.7 dB (bass 10). The effect is a bit smaller when the treble is high, because the knobs share one circuit.

treble_taper.label: Treble taper

choices.linear: Resistance changes evenly as you turn.
choices.log: Audio taper: at the half-way point only 10% of the resistance. Most of the change is at the top of the knob.

treble_taper.short: How the treble pot's resistance changes as you turn it (top_boost and james: log unless you set it).
treble_taper.tooltip: Real amps use either kind; the schematic says 'LIN' (linear, sometimes 'B') or 'LOG' (audio, sometimes 'A'). It changes where on the knob the sound changes most, not the range.

mid_taper.label: Middle taper

choices.linear: Resistance changes evenly as you turn.
choices.log: Audio taper: at the half-way point only 10% of the resistance.

mid_taper.short: How the mid pot's resistance changes as you turn it.
mid_taper.tooltip: See Treble taper. Check the schematic of the amp you copy.

bass_taper.label: Bass taper

choices.linear: Resistance changes evenly as you turn.
choices.log: Audio taper: at the half-way point only 10% of the resistance (the usual choice for bass pots).

bass_taper.short: How the bass pot's resistance changes as you turn it.
bass_taper.tooltip: See Treble taper. Bass pots are usually audio taper ('LOG' or 'A').

source_ohms.label: Source resistance
source_ohms.short: The output resistance of the tube stage that drives the tone stack.
source_ohms.tooltip: A cathode follower (most British and high-gain amps, and the 1959 tweed bass amp) drives the tone stack with about 1k: use 1000. A normal tube stage drives it from its plate, with roughly 30k-40k: the stack then loses more highs and the knobs behave differently (American 'blackface'-style amps). This setting copies that.

load_ohms.label: Load resistance
load_ohms.short: The resistance after the tone stack (usually the next tube's grid resistor or volume pot).
load_ohms.tooltip: Usually a 1M volume pot or grid resistor: use 1e6. A smaller load (for example a 250k volume pot) takes away some low end and volume.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: The tone stack loses about 5-20 dB like the real circuit (the stage after it in a real amp makes up for it). Raise this, or the drive of the next gain stage, to get the level back.

gate.label: Noise gate
gate.short: Turns the sound down when you stop playing, to remove hiss and hum.
gate.tooltip: High-gain amps make the small hiss and hum of a guitar very loud. The gate follows the signal level: when it falls below the threshold, the gate closes and turns the sound down; when you play again, it opens. Best use: put the gate at the START of the chain (where the guitar signal is clean and the hiss is quiet) and set 'Apply after' to the last gain stage (where the hiss is loud). Then the gate decides on the clean signal but mutes the loud hiss. A gate placed after a high-gain amp hears the amplified hiss as 'playing' and may never close.

threshold_db.label: Threshold
threshold_db.short: The gate opens when the signal is louder than this.
threshold_db.tooltip: Set it above the PEAKS of the hiss when you are not playing. Hiss peaks are about 10 dB above its average level, so hiss that measures -70 dB needs a threshold of about -55 dB. Too low: the gate stays open and the hiss gets through. Too high: quiet notes and the ends of ringing notes get cut off. At the start of the chain, typical values are -60 to -40 dB. Listen to the end of a ringing chord while you set it. The level the gate follows is the biggest peak in the last 20 ms, so it does not flicker between the peaks of a low note.

hysteresis_db.label: Hysteresis
hysteresis_db.short: The gate closes this many dB BELOW the threshold, so it does not flutter.
hysteresis_db.tooltip: A note that fades out slowly sits near the threshold for a while. If opening and closing happened at the same level, the gate would flutter open and shut ('chatter'). With 6 dB, the gate opens at the threshold but only closes when the level is 6 dB lower. Important: the closing point (threshold minus hysteresis) must still be above the hiss peaks, or the gate never closes. Measured with hiss at -70 dB and threshold -55 dB: 0 dB = the gate fluttered 4-8 times on one fading note; 3 dB = it opened once and closed once (clean); 6 dB = it never closed, because the closing point (-61 dB) was under the hiss peaks. If the gate does not close, lower this or raise the threshold.

attack_ms.label: Attack
attack_ms.short: How fast the gate opens when you play.
attack_ms.tooltip: Keep it very short (0.1-1 ms) so the pick attack is not lost. Longer values soften the start of every note, which can be a special effect (a 'swell').

hold_ms.label: Hold
hold_ms.short: How long the gate waits before closing.
hold_ms.tooltip: After the level falls below the closing point, the gate stays open for this long. It stops the gate from closing in the short gaps inside fast riffs. For tight staccato metal riffs: 10-30 ms. For normal playing: 50-150 ms.

release_ms.label: Release
release_ms.tooltip: Short (5-30 ms): very tight cut-offs for modern high-gain riffs, but ringing notes can end abruptly. Long (100-500 ms): notes fade out naturally, the hiss fades with them.

range_db.label: Range
range_db.short: How much the sound is turned down when the gate is closed.
range_db.tooltip: -80 dB = fully silent. -20 to -10 dB = the hiss is only made quieter, which sounds more natural, because a fully silent gate can make the starts and ends of notes stand out.

apply_after.label: Apply after
apply_after.short: Optional: the id of a later block. The gate listens here but mutes after that block.
apply_after.tooltip: Leave empty to gate the sound right here. Set it to the id of a later block (for example the last gain stage) to listen to the clean signal here but mute the loud hiss after that block. The sound passes through the gate's own position unchanged. The block must come after the gate and can not be inside a feedback loop (use the feedback block's own id instead).

split.label: Split
split.short: Parallel paths: the same sound goes through several chains side by side, then they are mixed.
split.tooltip: Lets an amp have more than one path. Examples: the 'jumpered' channels of old British amps (a bright channel and a normal channel mixed, each with its own volume); a clean signal blended under a high-gain sound to keep the pick attack; two cab IRs (or two microphones) mixed; a bass path and a treble path with different gain. Each path can hold any blocks.

paths.label: Paths
paths.short: The parallel chains. At least one.
paths.tooltip: Each path has its own chain, level and invert switch. All paths get the same input, and their outputs are added together.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.short: Volume after the paths are mixed.
level_db.tooltip: Adding paths together makes the sound louder (two equal paths = +6 dB). Use this to bring the level back, or to set how hard the mix drives the next gain stage.

eq.label: EQ
eq.short: Tone shaping with a list of filter bands.
eq.tooltip: Shapes the tone with any number of filter bands. Before a gain stage it decides which tones get clipped hardest. After a gain stage it works like the tone knobs of an amp. EQ adds no delay and no distortion.

bands.label: Bands
bands.short: The filter bands, applied one after another.
bands.tooltip: Add as many bands as you need. Each one is a high-pass, low-pass, low shelf, high shelf or peak. With no bands, the EQ only changes the level.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: Raises or lowers the volume of everything that comes out of this block. If the next block is a gain stage, this works like a gain knob: more level = more clipping in that stage.

gain.label: Gain stage
gain.short: One tube-like stage: filter, then drive into a clipping curve, then filter.
gain.tooltip: This is where the distortion happens. The sound goes: pre filters, then Drive pushes it into the clipping curve, then post filters, then Level. One stage with low drive = clean or edge of breakup. Two or three stages in a row with EQ between them = classic high-gain amps. The clipping is done at a higher sample rate (oversampling) so it does not sound harsh or fizzy.

linear.label: Linear (no clipping)
linear.short: The same stage without its non-linear parts, for comparing (X-ray listening uses it).
linear.tooltip: On: the curve becomes the straight line through the stage's working point, with the same slope: quiet playing sounds the same, but nothing clips, and there is no bias shift. Comparing a stage with its linear twin shows exactly what the clipping does; X-ray listening subtracts one from the other so you hear only that.

drive_db.label: Drive
drive_db.short: How hard the sound hits the clipping curve. More = more distortion.
drive_db.tooltip: The main gain knob of this stage. At 0 dB, a normal guitar signal stays almost clean. Around +12 dB: crunch. Around +24 dB: classic rock lead. +36 dB and more: high gain. More drive also means more compression: soft and loud notes come out closer in volume. Very high drive on one stage sounds fizzy; spreading the gain over several stages (with EQ between them) usually sounds better.

curve.label: Clipping curve

choices.soft: Smooth, round clipping (tanh). Warm and natural, both sides the same. Only odd harmonics. A safe start for any stage.
choices.tube: Uneven like a real triode: the top clips earlier and harder than the bottom. Adds even harmonics, which sound thicker and sweeter. Best for preamp stages.
choices.diode: Stays clean longer, then bends quickly. Sounds like a pedal with clipping diodes: tighter and more compressed than 'soft'.
choices.hard: Flat cut at the ceiling. Buzzy and aggressive, like a fuzz or a broken transistor. Best used with a low-pass after it.
choices.custom: Set the top and the bottom of the wave separately: where each side clips and how soft the bend is. Use it to copy a cathode follower (only the top clips), a pedal with uneven diodes, a fuzz, or anything else.
choices.triode: A real preamp tube (12AX7, 12AT7 or 12AU7) worked out from published tube equations, with its supply voltage, plate resistor and bias. The input is in volts at the grid. Small signals get mostly 2nd harmonic (the classic tube warmth); the top clips hard where grid current starts, the bottom squashes gradually toward cut-off.

curve.short: The shape of the clipping. Changes the character of the distortion.
curve.tooltip: All curves pass small signals unchanged and squash big ones. They differ in HOW they squash: soft and tube bend gradually (warm), diode bends late and fast (tight), hard cuts flat (buzzy). Uneven curves (tube, triode, custom with different sides, or any curve with Bias) add even harmonics. Measured with a 220 Hz note: soft = 0% 2nd and 6.7% 3rd harmonic; triode 12AX7 at 0.5 V = 2.6% 2nd and 0.1% 3rd; triode biased cold (-2.5 V) at 2 V = 24% 2nd harmonic.

top.label: Top level
top.short: Custom curve: where the top half of the wave clips.
top.tooltip: The highest level the top half of the wave can reach. Smaller = the top clips sooner. Making top and bottom different gives even harmonics (a thicker, more 'tube' sound). Example: a cathode follower clips only the top: top 1, bottom 20. Only used when Curve is 'custom'.

top_softness.label: Top softness
top_softness.short: Custom curve: how soft the top bend is. 0 = almost a hard corner, 1 = very gradual.
top_softness.tooltip: 0 = stays clean almost up to the level and then cuts nearly flat (diode-like, buzzy). 0.5 = a round bend, similar to a tube. 1 = starts squashing early and very gradually (smooth, compressed). Measured: at an input equal to the level, the output is 92% (softness 0), 78% (0.5), 50% (1) of the level. Only used when Curve is 'custom'.

bottom.label: Bottom level
bottom.short: Custom curve: where the bottom half of the wave clips.
bottom.tooltip: The lowest level the bottom half of the wave can reach (as a positive number). See Top level. Only used when Curve is 'custom'.

bottom_softness.label: Bottom softness
bottom_softness.short: Custom curve: how soft the bottom bend is.
bottom_softness.tooltip: See Top softness. Only used when Curve is 'custom'.

tube.label: Tube

choices.12AX7: The usual preamp tube: high gain (about 60 per stage with a 100k plate resistor). Used in almost every guitar amp preamp.
choices.12AT7: Medium gain (about 45). Often used in reverb drivers and phase inverters; cleaner and stiffer in a preamp.
choices.12AU7: Low gain (about 15). Lots of headroom; very clean. Used as a gentle first stage or a cathode follower.

tube.tooltip: Each tube has its own gain and curve shape. The numbers come from Koren's tube models (1996), which are widely used in tube simulation. Only used when Curve is 'triode'.

plate_v.label: Supply voltage
plate_v.short: Triode curve: the supply voltage at the top of the plate resistor.
plate_v.tooltip: Higher = more headroom, cleaner and louder. Lower = 'starved', clips sooner and more unevenly. Typical preamp supplies are 200-350 V. Measured: a 12AX7 with 100k and -1.5 V bias sits at 205 V on the plate with 300 V supply (about 1 mA, gain 61), like the real tube. Only used when Curve is 'triode'.

plate_ohms.label: Plate resistor
plate_ohms.short: Triode curve: the plate resistor (the stage's load).
plate_ohms.tooltip: 100k is the usual value. A bigger plate resistor gives a bit more gain and clips sooner; a smaller one gives more headroom. Copy it from the schematic (usually written like '100K' next to the tube's plate). Only used when Curve is 'triode'.

plate_volts.label: Real plate volts
plate_volts.short: Triode curve: output the real plate swing in volts (with the tube's real gain).
plate_volts.tooltip: Off: small signals come out the same size as they go in; only the clipping shape is the tube's. On: the output is the real voltage swing at the plate, so a 12AX7 stage turns 1 V into about 60 V, like in the real amp. Turn it on when you copy a schematic: then the next stage's Drive is simply the volume pot or divider between the two tubes (for example, an audio-taper volume pot at 5 is about -20 dB, at 7 about -12 dB). Only used when Curve is 'triode'.

bias_v.label: Bias voltage
bias_v.short: Triode curve: the grid voltage at rest (below 0). Sets how 'hot' or 'cold' the stage is.
bias_v.tooltip: The most important setting for the character of a tube stage. Around -1 to -1.5 V (a 1.5k cathode resistor in a real amp) = a normal 'hot' stage: the top clips first when the grid reaches 0 V (grid current). Around -2.5 to -4 V (a 10k cathode resistor) = a 'cold clipper': the bottom squashes very early, which gives a lot of 2nd harmonic and the tight, aggressive grind of many high-gain amps (measured: 24% 2nd harmonic at -2.5 V). In a real amp, bias voltage = cathode current x cathode resistor. Only used when Curve is 'triode'. With this curve, Drive sets how many volts reach the grid: a guitar gives about 0.1-1 V, earlier stages give many volts.

bias.label: Bias
bias.short: Moves the clipping point off center, so one side of the wave clips before the other.
bias.tooltip: At 0 both sides clip the same. Moving it away from 0 makes one side clip first, which adds even harmonics (a thicker, warmer, more 'tube' sound) and makes the distortion change as notes fade out. Small values (0.05-0.2) are subtle. Large values give a gated, sputtering 'cold' sound like a starved tube or a dying battery. The DC offset this creates is removed automatically.

bias_shift.label: Bias shift
bias_shift.short: How much a loud signal pushes the stage 'colder' for a moment. 0 = off.
bias_shift.tooltip: In a real tube stage, a signal that goes past the top of the curve makes the grid draw current. This charges the capacitor in front of the tube and moves its working point down (colder). After the loud part, it drifts back. You hear it as: right after a hard hit, soft notes come out quieter, thinner and a bit sputtery, then they 'open up' again. This is a big part of how cascaded high-gain amps feel and why they 'chug'. Measured with 1.0: a soft note right after a loud chord came out 35% quieter with 5 times more 2nd harmonic, and was back to normal after about 100 ms. 0 = off (a stiff, 'perfect' stage). 0.3-0.6 = a normal tube stage. 1.0 = strong, gated, 'farty' blocking when hit very hard. Works with any curve; it only does something when the stage is driven past the top of the curve.

shift_attack_ms.label: Shift attack
shift_attack_ms.short: How fast the working point moves when hit hard.
shift_attack_ms.tooltip: In a real stage the capacitor charges fast, through the low resistance of the conducting grid: around 0.5-2 ms. Shorter = the pick attack itself gets squashed. Longer = the first hit gets through, then the stage chokes. Only matters when Bias shift is above 0.

shift_release_ms.label: Shift release
shift_release_ms.short: How fast the working point comes back after a loud part. Empty = C x R of the coupling capacitor.
shift_release_ms.tooltip: In a real stage this is the coupling capacitor draining through the grid resistor (for example 22 nF x 1 Mohm = 22 ms). Short (10-30 ms): the stage recovers between notes; tight and fast. Long (100-500 ms): the stage stays choked after a hard hit; you hear a 'swell' as it recovers, and with fast palm mutes it sounds gated. Bigger coupling capacitors in a real amp = longer release. Only matters when Bias shift is above 0.

coupling_nf.label: Coupling capacitor
coupling_nf.short: The capacitor that brings the signal into this tube's grid. 0 = DC-coupled (no capacitor).
coupling_nf.tooltip: Every tube stage gets its signal through a capacitor into its grid resistor. Together they are a gentle (1st-order) high-pass at 1 / (2 pi R C): 22 nF into 1 Mohm = 7.2 Hz (passes all the bass), 1 nF into 1 Mohm = 160 Hz (a tight stage, as in many high-gain amps), 0.5 nF = 320 Hz. The SAME capacitor causes bias shift: when the grid is driven past 0 V it draws current and charges the capacitor, and the charge drains through the grid resistor, so the stage recovers in C x R (22 nF x 1 Mohm = 22 ms, 1 nF = 1 ms). That is why tight high-gain amps use small capacitors: they also recover fast instead of 'blocking'. 0 = no capacitor (DC-coupled, as from a stage into a cathode follower).

grid_ohms.label: Grid resistor
grid_ohms.short: The resistor from this tube's grid to ground (or the volume pot before it).
grid_ohms.tooltip: Usually 1 Mohm, 470k or 220k, or a 1 Mohm volume pot. With the coupling capacitor it sets the bass cut, 1 / (2 pi R C), and how fast bias shift recovers, C x R.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: Sets the output volume of this stage. Since the clipping curve already limits the peaks, Level is how you set how hard this stage drives the NEXT stage. It works like the coupling between two tubes.

pre.label: Pre filters
pre.short: Filters before the clipping. They decide what gets distorted.
pre.tooltip: This is the most powerful tone control in an amp. Cutting bass before the clipping (high-pass at 100-700 Hz) gives a tight, clear distortion that does not get muddy, like the small coupling capacitors in real preamps. Boosting mids before the clipping (peak at 700-1000 Hz) gives a singing, pushed-amp lead tone. Real tube stages often have a gentle high-shelf boost here (the 'bright cap').

post.label: Post filters
post.short: Filters after the clipping. They smooth the distorted sound.
post.tooltip: A low-pass after the clipping (5-10 kHz) removes fizz, like the natural top-end loss of real tube stages. A 10 Hz high-pass is always added at the end to remove DC offset; you do not need to add it.

oversample.label: Oversampling

choices.1: Off. Fastest. Harsh fold-back noise with heavy clipping.
choices.16: 16x. Only for extreme high gain with the 'hard' curve.

oversample.short: How many times faster the clipping runs, to avoid harsh noise.
oversample.tooltip: Clipping creates very high tones. Without oversampling, the ones above the top of the sample rate fold back down as harsh, out-of-tune noise (aliasing). Measured with hard clipping at 4.5 kHz: off = noise only 21 dB below the sound, 8x = 62 dB below (not audible). It does nothing now: the whole amp is oversampled once (the Quality menu), so this setting is only kept so older presets still load.

sag.label: Sag
sag.short: Power supply sag: playing hard lowers the clipping ceiling of other stages for a moment.
sag.tooltip: In a real tube amp, playing hard pulls current from the power supply, so its voltage drops for a moment and the tubes clip earlier. This gives the soft, 'squishy', touch-sensitive feel of old amps, and the 'bloom' when a chord rings out and the supply recovers. The sag block listens to the sound where it sits (the sound passes through unchanged) and lowers the ceiling of the gain stages listed in Targets. Usually placed right before the power amp stage.

amount.label: Amount
amount.short: How far the ceiling can drop. 0 = no sag, 0.5 = down to half.
amount.tooltip: 0 = a stiff modern supply (tight, punchy, solid-state rectifier). 0.2-0.3 = a normal tube amp. 0.4-0.6 = a vintage tube-rectified amp: very squishy and compressed, the note 'blooms' after the pick attack. Above 0.6 the sound pumps and breathes with your playing. Quiet playing is not changed at all, only playing that reaches the ceiling.

sens_db.label: Sensitivity
sens_db.short: How easily the sag reacts. Higher = reacts to softer playing.
sens_db.tooltip: Raises or lowers the signal the sag listens to (the sound itself is not changed). If the sag only kicks in on the very hardest hits, raise it. If even light playing makes the sound squash, lower it. The right value depends on how loud the signal is where the sag block sits.

attack_ms.label: Attack
attack_ms.short: How fast the ceiling drops when you hit hard.
attack_ms.tooltip: Short (1-5 ms): the sag grabs right away, and the pick attack gets squashed too. Longer (10-30 ms): the first hit gets through at full punch, then the note settles and compresses. Real amps are around 2-10 ms.

release_ms.label: Release
release_ms.short: How fast the ceiling comes back when you play softer.
release_ms.tooltip: This is how fast the power supply recovers. Short (50-100 ms): tight, follows fast playing. Medium (150-300 ms): the classic 'bloom', where a ringing chord slowly opens up as the supply recovers. Long (500 ms and more): the amp stays compressed for a while after a hard hit, and can 'pump' with the rhythm.

targets.label: Targets
targets.short: The ids of the gain and power blocks this sag controls.
targets.tooltip: List the gain stages and power amps that share this power supply. They must come after the sag block in the chain (one inside a later feedback block is fine). Usually the power amp: with a power block, sag lowers the supply voltage, which lowers both the tube current and the voltage swing, like a real power supply. Adding preamp stages too gives an even softer, more 'saggy' feel.

feedback.label: Feedback loop
feedback.short: A loop around a few blocks: part of the output is sent back and taken away from the input.
feedback.tooltip: Most tube power amps send part of the speaker signal back to an earlier stage (negative feedback). This lowers the gain, makes the clipping cleaner and tighter, tightens the bass, and makes the amp sound less raw. Amps with little or no feedback sound loose, raw and aggressive; amps with a lot sound tight, clean and polished. The filters in Path decide which tones get less feedback, so those come out louder: that is how Presence and Resonance knobs work. Put the power amp gain stage (and its EQ) inside the loop.

amount.label: Amount
amount.short: How much of the output is fed back. More = tighter, cleaner, less gain. Below 0 = positive feedback.
amount.tooltip: 0 = no feedback (raw, loose, like amps that have none). Small values (0.1-0.3) = most classic amps. Larger values = tight and polished, the clipping becomes harder at the edge (clean, then suddenly clipped). The gain drops as amount goes up, so raise the drive of the inner stages or the level to make up for it. Note: the effect also depends on the inner gain; the real loop gain is about amount x the gain of the inner chain. BELOW 0 = positive feedback: more gain and a harder, more compressed feel (a gain of 2 with amount -0.25 becomes 4). It only works while the loop can never gain 1 or more within one sample (a real circuit would then latch or howl): the preset says so with an error and the loop gain it found. Keep the inner gain small; the limit uses the steepest point of every inner block, so it is on the safe side.

path.label: Path filters
path.short: Filters on the feedback signal. Tones they cut get less feedback, so they come out LOUDER.
path.tooltip: This works the opposite way to a normal EQ: cutting a tone here makes it louder at the output, because that tone is no longer held back by the feedback. Presence: high shelf around 2-4 kHz with -6 to -12 dB = more bite and sparkle. Resonance (or Depth): low shelf around 80-120 Hz with a cut = bigger, looser bass, like a closed-back cab pushing back. With no filters, all tones get the same feedback.

chain.label: Inside the loop
chain.short: The blocks inside the loop (EQ, tone stack, gain stages and power amps only).
chain.tooltip: Usually the power amp stage, maybe with an EQ for the output transformer (a high-pass around 60-100 Hz and a low-pass around 5-8 kHz). Inner gain stages can not set their own oversampling: the whole loop runs at the loop's oversampling rate.

oversample.label: Oversampling

choices.1: Off. Fastest, harsh with heavy clipping.

oversample.short: How many times faster the whole loop runs.
oversample.tooltip: Same idea as in the gain stage: it keeps clipping inside the loop from making harsh noise. It does nothing now: the whole amp is oversampled once (the Quality menu); kept so older presets still load.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: Feedback lowers the volume. Use this to bring it back, so you can compare settings at the same loudness.

ir.label: Cab IR
ir.short: Speaker cabinet sound from an impulse response (.wav) file.
ir.tooltip: An impulse response (IR) is a short recording that captures how a speaker cabinet and microphone change the sound. Loading one makes the amp sound like it is played through that cab. The cab removes the harsh top end of the distortion, so without an IR (or a strong low-pass) a distorted amp sounds buzzy. Put this block last. It adds no delay. In the plugin, only eq and other ir blocks can come after it, and it can not be inside a split or feedback block (the plugin runs the cab at the normal sample rate, after the oversampled amp). If the file is not found, the plugin uses a built-in test cab and says so. The plugin's 'Load IR' button replaces the file of every ir block.

file.label: IR file
file.tooltip: Any mono or stereo .wav file (stereo is mixed to mono). If its sample rate is different from the amp's, it is converted automatically. Most IRs are 20-500 ms long; longer files can include room sound.

mix.label: Mix
mix.short: Blend between no cab (0) and full cab (1).
mix.tooltip: 1 = only the cab sound, the normal setting. Lower values let some of the raw amp signal through, which adds fizz and air. Useful to compare the sound with and without the cab, or to use a direct signal for a special effect.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: IR files have very different loudness. Use this to match the volume when switching between cabs, so you hear the tone difference and not the level difference.

room.label: Room (acoustic feedback)
room.short: The amp's sound goes back into the guitar's strings: notes sustain and bloom into feedback, as in front of a loud amp.
room.tooltip: In front of a loud amp, the sound from the speaker shakes the guitar's strings. They answer at the note you play and its harmonics, the pickup hears that, the amp makes it louder, and it goes round again. Loud enough, a note sustains forever and 'blooms' into one of its harmonics (which one depends on the distance: the sound's travel time decides which harmonic comes back in step). This block does that: put it LAST (after the cab). It follows the note you play with a pitch tracker (one note: with a chord it follows the strongest), and it treats the strings as muted when your input falls fast (a hand on the strings) or is very quiet, or when Feedback time is over after a pick. Those parts stand in for you; the rest is the physics of the loop. Why Feedback time: the feedback lives only inside the plugin. Your real string is not shaken by the amp, so it fades away slowly into your guitar's hum, and the plugin can not hear your hand stop it. Turn Volume up until notes start to sustain.

distance_m.label: Distance
distance_m.short: How far the guitar is from the speaker.
distance_m.tooltip: The sound needs distance / 343 m/s to arrive (0.5 m = 1.5 ms), and it gets 6 dB weaker at twice the distance. Moving changes WHICH harmonic the feedback blooms into, because the travel time decides which ones come back in step: walking around in front of the amp to find the sweet spot is real.

volume_db.label: Volume
volume_db.short: How loud the amp is in the room (at 1 m). Higher = more feedback.
volume_db.tooltip: How strongly the amp's sound pushes the strings at 1 m, relative to the plugin's normal output level. Low: notes only ring a bit longer. Higher: held notes sustain and bloom. Too high: everything howls. With the strings muted (your hand on them) nothing happens, as on a real amp.

sustain_s.label: String sustain
sustain_s.short: How long the string rings by itself (time to fall 60 dB).
sustain_s.tooltip: A solid-body guitar's string rings for several seconds; a hollow body or old strings less. The longer it rings by itself, the less push from the amp it needs to keep going.

string_tone_hz.label: String tone
string_tone_hz.short: Above this the string's harmonics die fast, so feedback blooms into the note or a low harmonic.
string_tone_hz.tooltip: A real string loses its high harmonics much faster than the note itself. In this model the string loses its highs above this frequency on every round trip (a gentle low-pass in the loop; the note stays in tune). Lower: the feedback stays on the note, the octave or the fifth. Higher: it can jump to high, squealing harmonics, most of all through a bright high-gain amp.

mute_db.label: Muted below
mute_db.short: Below this input level (in volts: 0 dBV = 1 V) the strings count as muted.
mute_db.tooltip: The plugin can not see your hand. So the strings count as muted when the input falls to a tenth within about 10 ms (a hand on the strings), or stays below this level. A guitar played hard gives about 0.5 V (-6 dBV). A guitar's hum is often above the default -60 dBV: then this never mutes, and only Feedback time stops the feedback. The In meter shows your level when you do not play.

feedback_s.label: Feedback time
feedback_s.short: How long the amp can keep a note going after you pick it. 60 (the top) = it never stops.
feedback_s.tooltip: After each pick attack the sound from the amp can push the string for this long. Then the string counts as muted, as if your hand were on it: the feedback dies in about 50 ms. Picking again starts the time again. It is needed because the feedback lives only inside the plugin: your real string fades away into your guitar's hum, so the plugin can not hear your hand. At 60 s (the top of the knob) it never stops by itself: only a fast drop of your input (a hand on loud strings) or silence below Muted below stops it.

harmonic.label: Ring at harmonic
harmonic.short: 1 = the whole string. 2, 3, ...: like a finger resting lightly at 1/2, 1/3 of the string: the feedback blooms into that harmonic.
harmonic.tooltip: A finger resting lightly on a string at 1/2 of its length stops every mode that moves there, so only the octave (and its multiples) can ring: a natural harmonic. At 1/3 it is the fifth above the octave (3x the note), at 1/4 two octaves up. Here the string rings only at that harmonic, so the feedback can only bloom into it. The loop still has to come back in step there, so the distance still matters, as in a real room.

find_spot.label: Find the spot
find_spot.short: Like a player who steps until the note blooms: the sound's arrival moves until the chosen harmonic comes back in step.
find_spot.tooltip: Players move in front of the amp until the feedback blooms into the harmonic they want. This does that: at the chosen harmonic (Ring at harmonic) it compares the sound coming back with what the string is ringing, and makes the sound arrive a little later or sooner (by at most one period of that harmonic, so the distance stays close to Distance) until they are in step, in about 100 ms. Like the pitch tracker, this stands in for the player; the rest is the loop's physics. The result is the same every time for the same playing.

strings.label: Sympathetic strings
strings.short: Extra strings tuned to fixed notes ring along with your playing: a halo in the key you play in, like a sitar's.
strings.tooltip: A sitar, a sarangi or a piano with its sustain pedal down has strings that nobody plays. Your playing shakes them through the bridge, and each one takes up only the energy that matches its own note and its harmonics. So playing in their key makes a ringing cloud that goes on after you stop, while notes that do not fit stay dry. Without a list of notes it uses a guitar's own open strings (E A D G B E), which ring along on a real guitar too. Before the amp it is like an acoustic instrument; after the amp, like a reverb that only rings in tune. All of it is the physics of the strings: nothing listens to what you play.

notes.label: Tuning
notes.short: The notes the strings are tuned to: names like D3, F#4, Bb2, or numbers in Hz.
notes.tooltip: One string per note. A4 = 440 Hz, C4 = middle C, E2 = a guitar's low E. A drone in your key works well (D2 A2 D3 A3 D4 for songs in D), or a whole scale for a sitar-like shimmer.

coupling_db.label: Coupling
coupling_db.short: How strongly your playing shakes the strings.
coupling_db.tooltip: Through the bridge only a little of your playing reaches each string, but it adds up period after period when the note fits. Higher = louder, faster halo.

sustain_s.label: String sustain
sustain_s.short: How long the strings ring at their notes (time to fall 60 dB).
sustain_s.tooltip: Long: a big halo that hangs on after you stop, and the strings take up only notes very close to their own. Short: a quick shimmer, less picky about tuning.

string_tone_hz.label: String tone
string_tone_hz.short: Above this the strings' harmonics die fast.
string_tone_hz.tooltip: Real strings lose their highs faster than their note. Lower = a darker, softer halo. (The strings stay in tune.)

mix_db.label: Mix
mix_db.short: How loud the strings are next to your own sound.
mix_db.tooltip: The strings' sound is added to the sound that comes in, which passes unchanged.

restring.label: Restring
restring.short: Play your guitar, hear a virtual string with physics you choose: lower, stiffer, longer, bending by itself.
restring.tooltip: Each pick attack plucks a virtual string with your own DI's last period, stretched to the new string's length, so where and how hard you pick carries over. Then the string rings on its own physics: transposed (a bass, a tiny high string), stiff like a piano or a bell (stretched harmonics), with any sustain, its pitch gliding back after each pluck. It follows your note while it rings (slides, bends, hammer-ons), and a hand on the strings stops it. Not physics, standing in for you: a pitch tracker finds your note, so a new note starts about 15-30 ms after the pick (like a guitar synth; lower notes take longer), and it follows one note (with a chord, the strongest). Put it first, before the amp.

transpose.label: Transpose
transpose.short: How far the virtual string is tuned from the note you play (12 = an octave).
transpose.tooltip: -12 turns the guitar into a bass, +12 or +24 into a mandolin-like tiny string. Fractions work too (microtones).

stretch_cents.label: Stiffness
stretch_cents.short: How stiff the string is: how many cents sharp its 10th harmonic is (0 = a perfect string).
stretch_cents.tooltip: A stiff string (thick, short, like a piano's bass strings) springs back on its own, so its higher harmonics come out sharp: harmonic n is at n f0 sqrt(1 + B n^2). This gives B: 1-9 cents = B 0.00001-0.0001 (guitar strings), 17-80 cents = B 0.0002-0.001 (most piano strings), hundreds = far stiffer than any string, towards a bar or a bell. The status line shows B. Modelled with 16 all-pass filters fitted over the first 20 harmonics up to 2.5 kHz (higher ones are only close).

sustain_s.label: Sustain
sustain_s.short: How long the note rings (time to fall 60 dB).
sustain_s.tooltip: Its own sustain, whatever your guitar does: 60 s rings on like an endless string, 0.3 s is a short muted pluck. It goes on after your guitar's note fades, until you stop the string with your hand or pick a new note.

string_tone_hz.label: String tone
string_tone_hz.short: Harmonics at this frequency fade 10 times as fast as the note.
string_tone_hz.tooltip: Real strings lose their highs faster than their note, in seconds, the same on every fret: the loss grows with the square of the frequency (twice the frequency, about 4 times as fast). Lower = a darker string whose pluck softens quickly. (The harmonics stay in tune. Below about 3 x the note this would need the string to GAIN energy at 0 Hz: then sustain_s wins and the highs fade less than asked.)

bend_semitones.label: Pluck bend
bend_semitones.short: Each pluck starts this far above the note, then glides back to it.
bend_semitones.tooltip: A hard pluck stretches a slack string, so it starts sharp and falls back (a few cents on a guitar, a lot on a loose bass or a koto). Negative = it starts flat and rises, which no real string does.

bend_s.label: Bend time
bend_s.short: How fast the pluck bend glides back (63% of the way in this time).
bend_s.tooltip: The bend falls as e^(-t / bend_s): after 3 x bend_s only 5% of it is left.

mix.label: Mix
mix.short: 1 = only the virtual string, 0 = only your guitar.
mix.tooltip: Output = (1 - mix) x your guitar + mix x the string. 0.5 = both, like a doubled instrument.

mute_db.label: Muted below
mute_db.short: Below this input level (0 dBV = 1 V) nothing counts as a note or a pick attack.
mute_db.tooltip: The plugin can not see your hand. A pick attack is the level jumping to twice where it was (and above this level); a hand on the strings is the input falling to a tenth within about 10 ms: the string then dies in 50 ms. A note fading away slowly does not stop it.

bow.label: Bow
bow.short: Your playing bows a virtual string: endless, swelling notes, with a real bow's scratch and squeak.
bow.tooltip: Your level is the bow's speed and force (both together), your note sets the string's length, a hand on the strings lifts the bow. The friction is solved exactly every sample: the string sticks to the bow, then slips back, once a period when it works (Helmholtz motion, what a violin does). Too little force: it slips several times a period (a whistly 'surface sound'). Too much: it can not let go in time and grinds (raucous). Where you put the bow changes both limits and the tone. The status line shows the most force for clean motion (Schelleng). Not physics, standing in for you: a pitch tracker finds your note (about 15-30 ms after the pick). Put it first, before the amp.

transpose.label: Transpose
transpose.short: How far the bowed string is tuned from the note you play (12 = an octave).
transpose.tooltip: -12 = a cello-like low string, +12 a violin-like high one.

bow_position.label: Bow position
bow_position.short: Where the bow sits: its distance from the bridge, as a share of the string.
bow_position.tooltip: Near the bridge (0.05, 'sul ponticello'): bright and glassy, needs more force but allows more. Far from it (0.3, 'sul tasto'): soft and flute-like, needs little force but chokes easily. Each period the string sticks for 1 - this share of the time.

bow_force_n.label: Bow force
bow_force_n.short: How hard the bow presses on the string at full playing level (0.5 V).
bow_force_n.tooltip: It scales with your level, like the speed, so softer playing stays in the same kind of motion. Clean motion needs a force between a least and a most (Schelleng); the most is 2 Z v / (bow position (static - dynamic friction)): 2.0 N with the defaults. Measured with the defaults: clean at 1.0 and 1.4-1.9 N (between, the start decides, as with a real bow). Near the most the pitch goes a little flat.

bow_speed.label: Bow speed
bow_speed.short: How fast the bow moves at full playing level (0.5 V).
bow_speed.tooltip: The string's swing grows with the bow speed. Faster also raises the most force for clean motion. A violinist uses about 0.05-1 m/s. The output is scaled so full playing stays about 0.5 V.

friction_static.label: Static friction
friction_static.short: How strongly the rosined bow holds the string while they move together.
friction_static.tooltip: The force it can hold = this x the bow force. Rosin: about 0.8.

friction_dynamic.label: Sliding friction
friction_dynamic.short: The friction while the string slides along the bow (fast sliding).
friction_dynamic.tooltip: Friction falls from the static value towards this one as the sliding gets faster (half way at 0.1 m/s). The gap between the two is what lets the string go and catch again: equal values = it never sticks.

swell_s.label: Bow attack
swell_s.short: How fast the bow gets up to your playing level.
swell_s.tooltip: Short: the note speaks at once, with a scratch. Long: it swells in like a slow bow stroke. The start decides which kind of motion the string falls into (Guettler).

release_s.label: Bow hold
release_s.short: How slowly the bow slows down after your note fades.
release_s.tooltip: The bow follows your level's peaks and falls back no faster than this (63% in this time). Long: one pluck becomes a long bowed note. A hand on the strings lifts the bow at once.

bridge_loss_db.label: Bridge loss
bridge_loss_db.short: How much of the wave goes into the body at each trip to the bridge.
bridge_loss_db.tooltip: The same share on every trip whatever the note, as on a real bowed instrument: so low notes ring longer. 0.55 dB = 1 s to fall 60 dB at 110 Hz. This loss per trip decides how cleanly the bow works: Raman's extra waves die by it.

string_tone_hz.label: String tone
string_tone_hz.short: Harmonics at this frequency lose 10 times as much at the bridge as the note.
string_tone_hz.tooltip: Lower = a darker string and a rounder corner in its motion. (The harmonics stay in tune.)

mix.label: Mix
mix.short: 1 = only the bowed string, 0 = only your guitar.
mix.tooltip: Output = (1 - mix) x your guitar + mix x the bowed string.

mute_db.label: Muted below
mute_db.short: Below this input level (0 dBV = 1 V) nothing counts as a note or a pick attack.
mute_db.tooltip: The plugin can not see your hand. A hand on the strings is the input falling to a tenth within about 10 ms: then the bow lifts and the string dies in 50 ms.

mouth.label: Mouth (talk box)
mouth.short: Your sound through a vocal tract: the guitar speaks vowels, oo-oh-ah-eh-ee, like a talk box.
mouth.tooltip: A talk box sends the amp's sound up a tube into the player's mouth, and the mouth's shape makes it speak. This is a vocal tract made of about 48 short tube sections: where the tube gets wider or narrower, part of the sound bounces back, and the tube's resonances (formants) make the vowel. Put it after the amp. Move Vowel by hand, from your DAW, or let Follow move it with your playing. The five vowel shapes are fitted to measured vowel formants (Peterson and Barney 1952, men), not measured tract shapes.

vowel.label: Vowel
vowel.short: The mouth's shape: 0 = oo, 1 = oh, 2 = ah, 3 = eh, 4 = ee (in between: a blend).
vowel.tooltip: Put it on the front panel and automate it, or sweep it like a wah. oo and oh round the lips (low formants), ee pushes the tongue forward (a high second formant).

follow.label: Follow
follow.short: How far your playing moves the vowel (in vowels, at the loudest you played lately).
follow.tooltip: 2 with Vowel at 0: each note says 'oo-ah' as you hit it and goes back to 'oo' as it fades. Negative = the other way. The level is measured against the loudest of the last few seconds, so it works at any volume.

follow_ms.label: Follow release
follow_ms.short: How fast the vowel goes back as a note fades.
follow_ms.tooltip: The level rises in 5 ms and falls back in this time (to 37%).

length_cm.label: Tract length
length_cm.short: How long the vocal tract is: 17 cm is a man's, 14.5 a woman's, 12 a child's.
length_cm.tooltip: All formants move together: half the length, twice the frequencies. Very long = a giant's voice. (It is made of whole sections, so it lands within 0.4 cm.)

mix.label: Mix
mix.short: 1 = only the mouth's sound, 0 = the sound that comes in.
mix.tooltip: Output = (1 - mix) x the input + mix x the mouth.

plugin.label: Plugin
plugin.short: Knobs of the plugin itself, around the amp.
plugin.tooltip: These are not part of a preset. They are saved with your DAW project.

input_db.label: Input
input_db.short: Level of your guitar before the amp.
input_db.tooltip: The amp presets expect a guitar that peaks at about 0.5 (-6 dBFS) on hard strums, like a normal DI track. If your audio interface records your guitar quieter, turn this up until hard strums peak around -6 dBFS; if it is louder, turn it down. This changes how hard you hit the amp, so it changes the distortion, like a hotter or weaker pickup. Stereo input is mixed to mono (the average of both sides): if your guitar is only on one side of a stereo track, the amp gets it 6 dB quieter, so use a mono track or add +6 dB here.

output_db.label: Output
output_db.short: Volume after the amp and cab.
output_db.tooltip: The plugin sets the volume of each preset automatically when it is loaded (a short test riff through the amp averages -20 dBFS), so presets come out about equally loud. Use this knob to set your own level on top. It does not change the tone.

quality.label: Quality

choices.2x: Lowest CPU use. Some harsh 'aliasing' noise on high-gain sounds.
choices.8x: Best: clean even with lots of distortion. Uses the most CPU.

quality.short: How much higher than the session sample rate the amp runs (oversampling).
quality.tooltip: Clipping makes very high harmonics. At the normal sample rate, the ones above the top of the hearing range fold back down as harsh, out-of-tune noise ('aliasing'). So the amp runs at a higher rate inside: 8x means 384 kHz in a 48 kHz session. The value is for 44.1/48 kHz sessions; at 88.2/96 kHz the plugin uses half of it, at 176.4/192 kHz a quarter, so the amp always runs at about the same rate and sounds the same. The oversampling adds a small delay (a few samples), which the DAW makes up for automatically. Changing it reloads the amp.

knob.label: Knob 1-8
knob.short: The front panel's knobs, for automation and MIDI control in your DAW.
knob.tooltip: Knob 1 is the first knob on the front panel, and so on. Your DAW always calls them Knob 1 to Knob 8, because their meaning changes with the preset; the plugin window shows the real names. Moving one changes the preset, so the amp is rebuilt: a moving knob updates the sound about 10 times a second. That is fine for slow changes, but too coarse for fast sweeps.
